newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Cocoa demand healthy but Europe grind may be flat.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa demand healthy but Europe grind may be flat.

text.p: Cocoa demand in Europe continues healthy but growth in origin processing and a pick-up in grindings at the end of 1995 will leave the grind in the fourth quarter of 1996 struggling to break even, analysts say.

"We've had a phenomenal performance over the last two quarters but that was partly due to lower grinds in the summer of 1995. Now we're comparing like with like and Europe as a whole will do well to beat the fourth quarter 1995 figure," a leading UK-based cocoa analyst told Reuters.
Grind data, used by the industry as a key barometer of cocoa demand, are due to be published by the main processing centres of the Netherlands, Germany and Britain this week.

But European Continental companies are finding competition fiercer, analysts said. More and more beans are being processed locally in the countries that grow them, particularly the world's leader Ivory Coast and Indonesia.
"I'd be surprised if Europe came in higher bearing that in mind. If it does, it's encouraging," the UK analyst said.
The Dutch grind, the largest in the world, is expected to be around five percent higher than Q4 1995's 93,619 tonnes.

Industry sources in Amsterdam point to good demand for all cocoa products -- particularly powder, which they say is still relatively cheap and benefits from making up a small part of the manufacturing costs of many products.
"We're seeing customers from all over the world willing to pay for the quality powder that's produced here," one said. "Demand is looking very good across the board."
But they add the growth may be partly tempered by the switch to more liquor processing by one Dutch plant. Despite this, a Dutch grind close to 100,000 tonnes is expected.
And the trend of increased grindings looks set to continue in the current season.

Louis Bensdorp, president of the Dutch Cocoa Association, said cocoa processing in the Netherlands should reach around 400,000 tonnes in the 1996/97 (Oct-Sept) season, with the growth in bulk shipments an increasingly significant factor.
But other countries will struggle to match 1995 totals.

The British grind is expected to be slightly lower, as processing has been dented by the temporary halt in operations at one of the Mars plants. Analysts said this could mean the grind coming in up to 10 percent down on 46,688 tonnes.
The German fourth quarter 1995 grind was relatively strong at 71,375 tonnes (the third quarter 1996 was 65,824 tonnes) and the 1996 fourth quarter could drop by some two percent.
Economic data also point to a weaker figure, although there may be some compensation from higher exports.
Domestic consumption was still at a low ebb but exports to eastern Europe and the former CIS republics have risen.

"The overall economy is not good but the chocolate side has been better. Sales within Germany have not been spectacular but the export side is better," said Karsten Keunecke, managing director of the German confectionery industry association BDS.

The apparent discrepancy between German import statistics and grind data which came to the fore duting the December ICCO (International Cocoa Association) meeting was still being investigated. Keunecke confirmed German authorities were looking into the matter, which may mean previous grind figures have to be upwardly revised, but he said no conclusions had yet been drawn.
